question: In 2023, the European Commission published ‘A comprehensive approach to mental health’, recognising the need to address mental health in EU institutions and Member States, and taking into account areas that go far beyond health, such as education, employment, digital policy, social inclusion and justice.

However, the current framework has limitations, such as the fact that Member State participation is voluntary, that temporary projects are relied on to respond to systemic challenges, and that there are no guarantees of continuity beyond 2026.

New initiatives are also needed to promote an approach based on prevention, community care, integration of mental health into all policy and stable funding for civil society and people with lived experience. What steps will the Commission take to integrate mental health into employment, education, youth, digitalisation and social policy?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.8.2026) Promoting good mental health across all policy areas is supported through the 2023 Communication on a comprehensive approach to mental health1. Under the flagship ‘Children Health 360’, a prevention toolkit is developed with UNICEF. The focus is currently on the implementation of the Communication, including related joint actions, such as MENTOR2 and PRISM3.

The Commission will focus on addressing the impact of digitalisation on youth mental health. On 16 June 2026, it published a flash Eurobarometer4 that informed the work of Commission President’s Special Panel on child safety online5. The co-Chairs’s recommendations6, published on 13 July 2026, are currently being reviewed.

Under the Digital Services Act7, very large online platforms and very large online search engines are obliged to assess and mitigate systemic risks, including risks to mental well-being. Research and innovation in this area are supported through a Horizon Europe call8.

As part of the envisaged Quality Jobs Act, the Commission is considering the area of occupational health and safety risks in the workplace, including psychosocial ones. The European Agency for Safety and Health at Work will carry out a campaign on mental health and psychosocial risks at work in 2026-2028.

Further support is provided through the EU Youth Strategy, Erasmus+ Youth, the European Solidarity Corps, the 2022 Council Recommendation on Pathways to School Success9 and the 2024 Wellbeing Guidelines10. Support is also provided through sport via #BeActive, the European Week of Sport, and through a planned Open Method of Coordination Group on mental health in sport.
